title: VB1-03539
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are brothers and sisters and are from the village of XXXX in XXXX, India. They claim refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act").1

The duty of this panel is to find if there is sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to determine that there is a "serious possibility"2 that the claimants would be persecuted, or that there are substantial grounds to believe that they would be tortured, or at risk of losing their lives or being subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they returned to India. This also means that it must not be possible to get protection from this persecution or risk from Indian authorities and, further, that there is no other place within India where they could live safely, and that it would be reasonable to do so, in the claimants' circumstances.

In coming to my decision, I have considered the testimony, the evidence and the written submissions by the claimants' counsel. With respect to the sister, I have also kept in mind the points raised in the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines or other Guidelines.3
The panel has decided that the neither claimant is a Convention Refugee or a person in need of protection.

The claimants' complete allegations are set out in answer to Question 31 of their respective Personal Information Form (PIF) and need not be repeated here in here. To summarize, the female claimant alleges that from XXXX 2010 until XXXX 2011, she worked as XXXX XXXX at the house of the village head ("Sarpanch"). After a couple of weeks of working there, on an evening when the Sarpanch's wife and children were way, the Sarpanch sexually assaulted her. Because of fear and financial needs, the female claimant continued to work there, and she was sexually assaulted on another three or four occasions.

In the third week of XXXX 2011, the female claimant's brother, i.e., the male claimant, brought lunch for his sister at Sarpanch's home. The Sarpanch's daughter was the only person at home and made sexual advances towards him. When he refused, she partially tore off her clothes, made noise and ran out of the home, pretending she was being sexually assaulted by the male claimant. The neighbours chased after the male claimant, assaulted him, took him to the Sarpanch's home and confined him to a safe place until the Sarpanch arrived. When the Sarpanch arrived, he continued to lock him up without food and water. Finally, with the help of his sister, the male claimant was freed and escaped to his friend's home until shortly before he left for Canada.

The Sarpanch became very angry when he learnt of the female claimant's role in freeing her brother. To punish her, the Sarpanch, the neighbours who had detained the brother and a friend who had arrived with the police jeep, all raped the female claimant. They also threatened to kill her if she told anyone about what had happened.

Both claimants allege that the Sarpanch and in the case of the female claimant, the other men who had raped her, want to find them and hurt them. They allege that because of the Sarpanch's money, connection and power, he can do this with impunity.

Since the claimants have been in Canada, the female claimant has been in a relationship with a man. She is pregnant and is expecting to give birth on or about XXXX XXXX, 2012. The female claimant also alleges that as an unwed Muslim mother, she will face a reasonable possibility of persecution at the hands of the society at large. Identity

The claimants' original passports and other identity documents were seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada, copies of which are in Exhibit 2. I find that the claimants have established their identity and nationality as citizens of India. They also have the same last name. I accept that they are brother and sister.

In the claimants' case, the most determinative issue is credibility. When I assess credibility, there are two principles that I follow: Firstly, when a claimant swears to the truthfulness of certain facts, this creates the presumption that what he or she is saying is true unless there is reason to doubt it.4 Secondly, when assessing credibility the panel is entitled to rely on its rationality and common sense.5In this case I find that there is reason to doubt the claimants' truthfulness for the reasons on which I will elaborate. The Female claimant

The female claimant alleges that she met her current boyfriend, XXXX, in 2009 in the village. She testified that she met him while walking on the street. XXXX told her that he was going to Canada and provided her with his coordinates. The female claimant testified that she and XXXX did not start a friendship or an acquaintance then, and that their friendship and later relationship started and grew in Canada. The female claimant testified that she called XXXX when she was still in India and had obtained her Canadian visa, and told XXXX that she was traveling to Canada. It was XXXX who went to the airport and picked her up.

The female claimant also alleges that during the events of XXXX 2011, one of the men who sexually assaulted her was a man by the name of XXXX, who was XXXX's brother. The female claimant provided this evidence in the context of establishing that an assault she suffered in Canada by XXXX's sons6 was related to her ordeal in India.

The female claimant was asked why she was interested to call XXXX shortly after she was raped under horribly intimidating circumstances by his brother, particularly when she did not know XXXX well at the time. She testified that he when she had talked to XXXX, she thought he would be a good man and that he would not be partial. In light of the fact that the female claimant had earlier testified she had not formed a friendship with XXXX in India, I find the claimant's answer to be unreasonable and to lack credibility and common sense.

The female claimant also testified that XXXX is still married to another woman, but that he had separated from her before the claimant arrived in Canada. The claimant and XXXX first started a friendship, and after they were attacked by XXXX's relatives, they moved in together and started a romantic relationship. They now expect to have a baby together. The claimant testified that she believed she was attacked in Vancouver on the order of XXXX's brother, XXXX, and the Sarpanch, in continuation of what had happened in India. She stated, and it is marked on the police report, that XXXX's wife, XXXX's daughter, and his two nephews, assaulted the claimant.7 The claimant was asked what made her think the assault was related to the events in India and not because XXXX's wife was angry enough at her husband's friendship/relationship with her to have mobilized the assault. The claimant stated she knew the two assaults were related because XXXX's and the Sarpanch's children are in Canada, and that XXXX's sons, who were also XXXX's nephews, were involved in the attack. I do not find the claimant's answer to be reasonable or credible.

I note that the claimant never informed the police in her statement that she suspected the assault to have been related to a previous criminal act against her in India. When asked why, the claimant stated the police had never asked her the question. The police could not have been reasonably expected to have known the detailed background and relationship between the parties back in India. I therefore do not find the claimant's answer to be reasonable or credible.

Finally, the claimant testified that she came to Canada because she was afraid for her life in India. She was then asked why she did not make a refugee claim until approximately four months after her arrival in Canada. The claimant stated she did not know about refugee claims in Canada. I do not find her answer to be reasonable. The claimant had contacted XXXX, who lived in Canada, from India. She said that she left India because she was afraid for her life. One would reasonably expect that with her Canadian connection, she would at least attempt to learn about her options in Canada in less than a four month period. I find that the delay to be consistent with the claimant's lack of credibility and subjective fear.

I note that during the hearing, if the female claimant was asked a direct question on her PIF narrative, she would provide a consistent answer. However, when she was asked a question about the surrounding circumstances or events, she became evasive and provided long and unclear answers that required multiple repetitions. Her answers were also prone to exaggerations. For example, she stated that she believed the Sarpanch and the others would immediately kill her upon finding her. I also note that the claimant's detached demeanour was also inconsistent with what is reasonably expected of someone of the claimant's profile who had lived through her alleged experiences. More importantly, she stated that she never told a doctor about her multiple rapes, even in Canada when she has access to medical care, and in fact, she receives it as part of her pre-natal care.8 In short, I do not have sufficient credible evidence that the claimant experienced what she alleges happened in India.

The issue now becomes whether the female claimant will face a reasonable possibility of persecution in India because of the fact that she will have a child with XXXX and that she was not married to him. The panel asked whether she and XXXX had discussed whether he would return with her to India, if she was forced to do so. She said that they had never discussed it. The claimant testified that XXXX was also a Muslim, and that under Muslim religious laws, he could get married to up to four wives. The panel asked whether she and XXXX had considered marriage as an option. She stated that they had not discussed it because in Canada, there was no need to do it. While the panel does not expect the claimant to have found becoming a second wife as a respectable or viable option, the panel was surprised that the claimant did not express any objection in principle to being a second wife. The claimant alleges that she would face persecution at the hands of individuals in India who would not approve of her not being married. In light of this, I find the fact that the claimant had not even thought of marriage, and had therefore never discussed it with XXXX, when she testified marriage would be religiously permissible and not objectionable to her, to be inconsistent with a well founded fear of persecution.

The female claimant also testified that she did not know whether XXXX and his first wife were in the process of divorce. Given that her own fear of persecution is in part linked to being perceived to be a single mother, I find her lack of diligence in even learning about his potential divorce to be inconsistent with her allegations of fear. XXXX is also from India. The onus is on the claimant to demonstrate that she would face a reasonable possibility of persecution as a single mother in India. Yet, she never even asked XXXX to testify at the hearing to cast some light in what she did not know. Given the limited communication between the claimant and XXXX about their future together in India, I do not have sufficient credible evidence that the claimant would likely return to India as a single woman/mother.

I am mindful of the fact that elements necessary to establish a claim under s. 97 (1) are not identical to those necessary to establish whether a person is a Convention refugee under s. 96 of the Act. Consequently, as noted by the court in Bouaouni, a "... negative credibility determination, which may be determinative of a refugee claim under s. 96 of the Act, is not necessarily determinative of a claim under subsection 97 (1) of the Act."9 However, in the case at hand I do not have sufficient credible evidence that would provide a foundation for establishing a personal "risk" for the claimant pursuant to s. 97 (1) of the Act. The Male Claimant

The female claimant had testified that the Sarpanch and his wife were financially generous with her. She also testified that her own family's financial means were very limited, and the fact that the Sarpanch provided the family with a buffalo, which made a marked difference in their ability to eat nutritious dairy product. She was therefore asked why her brother would bring her food from home when she lived at the Sarpanch's and the family had limited ability to feed her. First, the female claimant stated that the Sarpanch family would only provide her with dinner. Then, she said she could also eat lunch there, but that her mommy would send her food from home. The brother was asked how often he would take food for his sister. He said that he could not remember, and that it varied greatly. I do not find the claimants' evasive and vague responses to be credible. I do not have sufficient credible evidence that the female claimant would sometimes eat lunch from her family home and that the brother would then take it to her.

The male claimant alleges that in late XXXX 2011, when he took lunch to his sister, the Sarpanch's older daughter opened the door and made sexual advances towards him. When he refused, she pretended that the male claimant had attempted to sexually assault her. The male claimant was asked questions about how sexual behaviour is perceived in his village, and whether or not males and females faced a similar stigma. The male claimant's answer to these points was very vague and evasive. He ultimately testified that males and females who had pre-marital sexual contacts faced equal stigma, and that whoever came from a more powerful family, could do what they wanted against the other. I find the claimant to have been evasive and to lack credibility.

The male claimant was asked whether there are formal charges pending against him. He stated that there were not because the Sarpanch family did not want to make it public that their daughter was implicated in a sexual assault case. However, he later testified that everybody in the village thought that he had tried to rape the Sarpanch's daughter. If everybody knows about the incident, then it would make no sense for the Sarpanch's family to not want to press charges to protect their daughter. I find the claimant's answer to lack credibility. I would therefore make an adverse inference that there is no objective documentary evidence, such as evidence that the claimant has been charged.10

Even if I accept the male claimant's allegations, I still find that he has a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) outside of his village in cities such as Ganhinagar, Jaipur or Delhi. This issue was raised with the claimant both before and at the hearing.

To find a viable IFA, the panel must be satisfied that (1) there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted or, on the balance of probabilities, in danger of torture or subjected to a risk to life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the IFA11 and (2) that conditions in that part of the country are such that it would be reasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.12

With respect to the burden of proof, in Rasaratnam,13 the Court of Appeal held that once IFA is raised as an issue, the onus is on the claimant to show that he or she does not have an IFA. The burden placed on the claimant is fairly high in order to show that the IFA is unreasonable. The Federal Court of Appeal in this case stated that the test to show that the IFA is unreasonable requires nothing less than the existence of conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of het claimant in relocating to a safe place. Actual and concrete evidence of adverse conditions is required.

The claimants testified that their village has approximately XXXX XXXX XXXX inhabitants. The claimants were asked how the Sarpanch of such a village could find them elsewhere in India. The claimants testified that with money and power, everything was possible in India. I note that the male claimant allegedly escaped from the Sarpanch home to a friend's home in another village in XXXX, stayed there for a few weeks until he came to Canada, and the Sarpanch still did not find him. The female claimant had testified that one of her rapists was a XXXX XXXX. For reasons I have explained, I have not found her to be credible. However, even if I were to accept this evidence, this would not credibly establish that the Sarpanch connections to a XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX would reasonably get him very far with information outside of XXXX.

The male claimant alleges he was never charged with any crime in relation to the accusations of sexual assault against him. In this case, the claimant is not a wanted man as a criminal, and as such, he will not face a risk of arrest by officials in cities such as Ganhinagar, Jaipur or Delhi. Moreover, a central registry does not exist in India.14 At most, some states have a registry. I do not have sufficient credible evidence that the Sarpanch has the means of monitoring it. Even in that case, both Japur and Delhi are cities outside of XXXX. I find that it will be unlikely that the claimant would face a reasonable possibility of persecution, or a personal risk of harm in a city such as Delhi.

The female claimant alleges that if the claimants are forced to return to India, the Sarpanch's and XXXX's family members in Vancouver would notify XXXX and the Sarpanch of the claimants' return. If the male claimant also believes this, nothing is preventing him to move away from Vancouver while he is in Canada. This way, the family cannot know when he has returned to India to report back to the Sarpanch. Further, even if the Sarpanch knows that the claimant has left Vancouver for India, I find I do not have sufficient credible evidence that he could find the claimant in a large country of over a billion people.

The claimant was asked why he could not relocate to a city such as Delhi, and he stated that with his low level of education, he could not live anywhere outside of his village. The claimant is a young man who has travelled half way across the world to Canada. Even though he has not passed his grade 12 exams, he has gone to school until grade 12. He is therefore fully literate. In Canada, he works in XXXX and he said he could communicate with coworkers and customers in English. I do not find his assertion that he cannot live anywhere outside of his village in India to be reasonable or credible.

Further, as stated above,15 the burden on the claimant to establish that the IFA is unreasonable is rather high. The claimant has not led sufficient credible evidence to discharge this burden. Having considered the conditions in Delhi and all the circumstances of this case, including those particular to the claimant, I find that it is not objectively unreasonable for the claimant to seek refuge there.
Since having a viable IFA is fatal to claims made under both ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Act, I find that the male claimant's claim under both sections fails.

For these reasons I determine that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
